title: Temper-Then-Tilt: Principled Unlearning for Generative Models through Tempering and Classifier Guidance
claim: A frozen base model is unlearned by training a light classifier head and combining its output with tempered logits at inference.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right; color-coded training (blue) and inference (gold) paths
description: A single left-to-right architecture diagram. On the left, input tokens feed a black Transformer block that outputs hidden states H1…HL. The hidden states feed a large rounded blue box labeled 'T3-Unlearning Classifier'. Inside it, Mean Pooling leads to two shaded trapezoids (A_phi, B_phi, a low-rank linear head) and then a Sigmoid, producing g_phi(x) in [0,1]^|V|. A blue arrow goes to a 'Classifier Loss' box at the top right, which takes the next token y and the selector label s. A gold inference path runs along the bottom and right: LM Head, then Tempering (1/T ln p), then a ln and a plus node that adds the classifier output, then Sample. Color separates training (blue) from inference (gold). Math labels sit under the arrows.
caption: T3-Unlearning for LLMs. We freeze the base model and train a linear head (shaded) on pooled hidden states to predict the vector gϕ(x) of class posteriors for all possible next tokens. In training, we apply the loss to the entry [gϕ(x)]y corresponding to the estimator of the class posterior P (s = 1 | x, y), while the entire vector gϕ(x) tilts the base model’s tempered logits for inference.
abstract: We study machine unlearning in large generative models by framing the task as density ratio estimation to a target distribution rather than supervised fine-tuning. While classifier guidance is a standard approach for approximating this ratio and can succeed in general, we show it can fail to faithfully unlearn with finite samples when the forget set represents a sharp, concentrated data distribution. To address this, we introduce Temper-Then-Tilt Unlearning (T3-Unlearning), which freezes the base model and applies a two-step inference procedure: (i) tempering the base distribution to flatten high-confidence spikes, and (ii) tilting the tempered distribution using a lightweight classifier trained to distinguish retain from forget samples. Our theoretical analysis provides finite-sample guarantees linking the surrogate classifier's risk to unlearning error, proving that tempering is necessary to successfully unlearn for concentrated distributions. Empirical evaluations on the TOFU benchmark show that T3-Unlearning improves forget quality and generative utility over existing baselines, while training only a fraction of the parameters with a minimal runtime.
